terms.gloss: to parse, to say what part of speech each word is
evidence: Quint. 1.8.13: ut partēs ōrātiōnis reddī sibi solūtō versū dēsīderet
terms.comment: Quintilian’s grammarian, reading a poem with his pupils, has them break up the verse and give back the parts of speech. Literally “to render the parts of speech”.

terms.gloss: to parse, to describe the properties of a word
terms.grammar: with the genitive of the word: proprietātēs nōminis, verbī
terms.comment: Traupman’s phrase: Dēscrībe proprietātēs «magister» nōminis, parse the noun “magister” (223). Classically proprietās verbōrum is the proper sense of words (Quintilian, Lewis & Short); we have not found the phrase for parsing.

phrases.latin: in praelegendō grammaticus et illa quidem minōra praestāre dēbēbit, ut partēs ōrātiōnis reddī sibi solūtō versū dēsīderet et pedum proprietātēs
phrases.english: in reading aloud first, the grammarian must also see to smaller things: when the verse has been broken up, he should require the parts of speech to be given back to him, and the qualities of the feet

phrases.latin: Dēscrībāmus nunc proprietātēs dictiōnum in hāc sententiā.
phrases.english: Let us now parse the words of this sentence.

sources: Lewis & Short: pars · Lewis & Short: oratio · Lewis & Short: reddo · Lewis & Short: proprietas · Lewis & Short: describo
John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency (printed page numbers): p. 223, p. 238, p. 248.
